extracted.subtask_description: Advice for using food and meals as tools for character development and worldbuilding in fantasy and science fiction; covers provenance, production, ritual, realism, and avoiding clichés. Intended to help writers craft meaningful, believable food scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food must matter to a character
rubrics_metrics.description: Food matters to a character; whether it’s a good memory or a bad memory, you should show why it matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t just list what’s in the dish — show what about the cooking, the communal preparation, or the occasion connects to the character’s history, emotions, or relationships. Use food memories to reveal character (e.g., Saturday preparation rituals, sharing comfort foods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meals should have meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Meals should have meaning — they should tell us something about the world or the character, not just show that they ate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid scenes that exist solely to show eating. Make meals serve narrative purposes (character-building, cultural exposition, plot relevance). Examples: ritualized meals, foods that mark class, foods that trigger memories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid generic 'soup stone' or 'intestine stuffing' descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the soup stone and stew, that we just ate, scene — don’t fall back on generic or filler descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: 'we threw some protein in a soup stone and it was delicious' or flat descriptions that are merely 'intestine stuffing' (Amal's phrase). Instead, make descriptions 'nourishing'—specific, purposeful, and revealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food as central metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: Food and eating are central metaphors that you can use to share things about a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use food scenes to express larger themes, anxieties, belonging, identity, or cultural change (e.g., sharing an immigrant’s home food to show belonging or exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Show provenance and history of food
rubrics_metrics.description: Food has history; food comes from places. Describe the history and provenance of a fictional meal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask where ingredients come from, how the dish evolved, whether recipes are time-locked by waves of immigration, and what historical/trade implications (e.g., presence of potatoes implies sea exploration) the ingredients suggest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for production and logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Think about the production behind the food — why certain animals/crops are raised and how environment and agriculture shape diets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ecology, climate, arability, and food management (e.g., raising cattle vs. crops because land is arid). Use this logic to deepen worldbuilding (links to empire, colonialism, class, power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be realistic about availability and preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Don’t put ingredients or elaborate preparations in improbable contexts without accounting for logistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for anachronisms and impossibilities (e.g., potatoes in pre-Columbian Europe). Consider cooking time, tools, foraging vs. preservation, and whether characters on the road could reasonably make long stews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid biological/physiological implausibilities (rabbit starvation example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of physiological realities (e.g., rabbit starvation when diets are too lean).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small factual details like lean-meat nutrition can break immersion if ignored (Samwise with rabbits and potatoes example). Use such facts to add verisimilitude or deliberately subvert them with explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ritual and presentation to convey meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The ritual of food — preparation, presentation, consumption — carries meaning and builds culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight rituals (who cooks, communal preparations, special plates/servings) to signal social structures, religious practice, family bonds, or status. Ritual increases the meal’s narrative weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let meals indicate socioeconomic status
rubrics_metrics.description: What people eat (banquet vs. meager rations) signals wealth, scarcity, and social conditions in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banquets imply wealth and abundance; minimal rations imply scarcity or class differences. Use these cues deliberately to shade setting and plot (e.g., diet-triggered anxieties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict immigrant/time-locked cuisines faithfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Immigrant cuisines can be time-locked — the food migrants bring reflects the era they left, and different waves bring different variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to create cultural texture: characters’ home cooking may differ from contemporary cuisine in the origin country. Show adaptation to available ingredients and the layering of culinary histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make future foods culturally rooted and palatable
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid depicting future food as only 'mush' or pills; future cuisines should be rooted in culture and palatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagine how cultures that go into space would adapt their cuisines; blend new production methods with cultural tastes (e.g., Expanse-style yeast/space-grown products). Avoid one-dimensional grotesque alien-food portrayals; show cultural exchange and hospitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alien/foreign foods should be experiential, not merely disgusting
rubrics_metrics.description: When depicting alien or foreign food (e.g., Klingon), present it as an experience and part of hospitality/culture rather than only as horror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show characters who love and take pleasure in those foods to normalize them (example: Bashir enjoying Klingon stall food). This conveys multiculturalism and reduces caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific sensory details to evoke emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific sensory memories (warm toasted bread and butter and jam) create powerful emotional beats linked to food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete sensory description (temperature, texture, smell) tied to a character’s emotional state multiplies resonance. Even small, simple foods can be vivid if tied to feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid defaulting to Western/modern assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful of unconsciously projecting modern/Western food norms into other cultures or historical settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research ingredient histories and cultural practices; don’t assume global ubiquity of certain foods. If you include them, provide worldbuilding justification (trade, exploration, colonization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make food scenes do narrative work beyond aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Food scenes should do more than look delicious — they should contribute to character, plot, or world information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer scenes where food reveals relationships, power dynamics, cultural norms, or catalyzes events, rather than existing as mere appetite stimulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of tone when using food for comedy or shock
rubrics_metrics.description: Food can be used for humor or shock, but be deliberate about why (e.g., jokes about cooking, or using gross dishes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance comedic beats with empathy; avoid cheap grotesque shock that undermines character depth. Use cultural context to frame humor respectfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework exercise: invent a fictional meal with provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Imagine a fictional meal, describe its history and provenance, and work that into a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write a mini story that tracks how the meal came together, what cultures/availability/restrictions produced it, and what the meal means to those characters—this practice enforces the above principles.
